newsitem.title: USA: Mercantile's shares climb on report of takeover bid.
newsitem.headline: Mercantile's shares climb on report of takeover bid.

text.p: Shares of Mercantile Stores Co. Inc. rose 10 percent Friday on a report that the department store chain has received a takeover bid from rival Federated Department Stores Inc.
The latest issue of Business Week cited a "New York banker" as saying that Mercantile received and rejected an offer of $75 a share from Federated, which owns Bloomingdale's and Macy's.
Fairfield, Ohio-based Mercantile, which operates Maison Blanche, J.B. White, McAlpin's and Gayfers stores, was not immediately available to comment on the report.
Mercantile's shares rose $5.625 to $62.375 on the New York Stock Exchange in late trading. Federated edged up 43.75 cents to $35.4375, also on the NYSE.

The 102-store chain has been on the radar screen of several retailers, including Federated, May Department Stores Co. and Dillard's Inc. for several years, Wall Street analysts said. But Mercantile has not agreed to a marriage, either because the offers it has received were too low or the Milliken family, which owns 40 percent of the company, could not iron out estate planning issues.

"I think Mercantile could be bought," said Walter Loeb, a retail industry consultant in New York. "Roger Milliken had negotiated with May at one point. But Mercantile wanted a hefty premium over the stock price."
Cincinnati-based Federated said it does not comment on rumours. May Department Stores Co. of St. Louis, parent of Lord & Taylor and Famous-Barr stores, also would not comment.
Roger Milliken, his brother Gerrish Milliken and cousin Minot Milliken own 40 percent of Mercantile and are members of the company's board, according to government filings.

Three years ago, Mercantile's shares soared when it issued a statement that it was negotiating a possible business combination. May was widely believed to be the suitor, but the talks apparently collapsed on a disagreement over price.
About a month later, Mercantile's shares climbed again, and Dillard was thought to be mulling a bid. But nothing happened.

Some analysts said the Milliken family was unlikely to accept a deal unless it received a rich premium over the stock's existing price to help cover tax liabilities or unless there was a change in capital gains tax laws.
Minot and Roger Milliken were both 81 and Gerrish was 79 years old at the time the company filed its proxy statement with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in April.
